name: TempleOS
summary: Public domain 64-bit operating system designed by Terry A. Davis as a self-contained recreational computing environment, running entirely in Ring 0 with the HolyC language and a 640x480 display in 16 colours.
license: Public Domain (fully open source code, free of rights)

content.introduction: TempleOS is a singular x86-64 operating system designed and programmed entirely by the American developer Terry A. Davis (1969-2018) over a period of about ten years, until 2013. Initially known under the names J Operating System, LoseThos then SparrowOS before adopting its definitive name in 2013, the project was developed alone and represents more than 100,000 lines of code. Designed as a spiritual and digital reinterpretation of the direct and unmediated computing of the Commodore 64 era, TempleOS aims to offer a programming and leisure environment without the layers of complexity of contemporary systems.
content.what_is_it: Technically, TempleOS is neither a Linux distribution nor a Unix-type operating system: it is a stand-alone 64-bit system resting on a single address space (SAS) architecture. The whole system, kernel, device managers, compiler, graphical environment and user programs, runs with the highest CPU privileges of supervisor mode (Ring 0). Physical memory is mapped directly onto the memory space without paging protection or virtualisation, allowing any instruction to access the internal structures of the hardware without an intermediary.
content.kernel_architecture_and_cooperative_mult: The TempleOS kernel adopts a cooperative multitasking model: each task holds the processor until it voluntarily hands control back to the scheduler (`Yield()`), eliminating synchronisation and preemptive context switch overheads. The multi-core architecture rests on an asymmetric Master-Slave organisation: processor core Core 0 orchestrates the system and distributes computing units to the other available CPU cores. This model guarantees ultra-low execution latency and predictable performance for real-time animations and graphical computations.
content.holyc_compiler_and_doldoc_document_archi: The system is articulated around a bespoke programming language, **HolyC**, a typed and compiled dialect derived from C/C++. The HolyC compiler is integrated into the heart of the system and works in JIT (Just-In-Time) and AOT (Ahead-Of-Time) mode. The shell command interpreter is in fact the HolyC compiler itself: each command typed on the keyboard is immediately compiled into native x86-64 machine code and executed. Text display relies on the **DolDoc** technology, which substitutes for plain ASCII text a structured rich format allowing hypertext links, trees, macros and even vector 3D models directly interactive and rotatable inside the source code.
content.graphics_audio_and_redsea_filesystem: By immutable design principle, TempleOS deliberately freezes its multimedia specifications: graphical display is strictly calibrated on a resolution of **640x480 pixels in 16 colours** (standard VGA palette) with direct access to the matrix video buffer (framebuffer) at 60 frames per second. Sound generation is exclusively assigned to the internal speaker of the motherboard (8-bit PC Speaker), the creator formally refusing to integrate complex sound card drivers or MIDI protocols. Storage rests on the native **RedSea** file system, a flat and contiguous system (without file fragmentation) supporting LZW block compression, complemented by reading ISO 9660 optical disk images.
content.hardware_requirements_and_historical_con: TempleOS requires an x86-64 64-bit processor, a minimum of 512 MB of RAM, ATA/IDE disk controllers and a keyboard/mouse with the PS/2 protocol (native or emulated by the BIOS). By deliberate design choice, the system has no network stack (no Internet connection, no TCP/IP) and no printer support. It runs optimally within virtual machines (QEMU, VirtualBox, VMware) or on old physical workstations with legacy BIOS compatibility. Placed in the public domain by Terry A. Davis, the system is delivered with its full source code and constitutes a major heritage study object in the history of independent computing.
content.release_history_and_dating: The sources do not agree on the start date: the official site gives none, the Wikipedia article places the J Operating System in 2005, and the initial presentation of this record retained a period of about ten years. The last published version is 5.03, dated 20 November 2017 according to the secondary source; no later version is referenced, development having stopped with the death of its author in 2018.
content.licensing_and_preservation: The official site presents TempleOS as a free 64-bit operating system placed in the public domain, and specifies that all content related to Terry A. Davis, TempleOS, J Operating System, SparrowOS and LoseThos must be considered as falling within the public domain. Distribution relies on external archives: Archive.org, Odysee, a torrent and a magnet link, as well as video rebroadcasts. The templeos.org domain is maintained by a third party and does not constitute an official development repository.
content.community_and_forks: The site lists the active communities: Reddit, a Discord server, Revolt, the IRC channel #templeos on Rizon and a Steam server, and cites ZealOS among the forks of the system. It specifies that these links do not constitute approval. No official code repository or contribution programme is maintained, development having stopped since the death of its author in 2018.
content.differences_with_other_systems: TempleOS does not separate kernel space and user space: the whole system runs in ring 0 in a single address space, without protected paging, which distinguishes it from Unix and Windows systems. Its scheduler is cooperative and not preemptive, the display is frozen at 640x480 pixels in 16 colours and sound is limited to the internal speaker. Unlike FreeDOS, it targets x86-64 exclusively and provides no network stack.
advantages: Remarkable software engineering work of more than 100,000 lines of code written from scratch by a single developer.
Direct and unmediated access to computer hardware in supervisor mode (Ring 0) without a virtualisation barrier.
Elegant HolyC language and native JIT/AOT compiler integrated into the shell with instant responsiveness.
Revolutionary DolDoc format integrating hypertext links, macros and 3D models directly into the source code.
Near-instant boot and extremely modest system resource consumption.
Source code fully open, documented and placed without any restriction in the public domain.
disadvantages: Official development stopped following the death of its creator in 2018 (system now a heritage item).
Total absence of memory protection: an erroneous pointer can instantly corrupt the entire system.
Deliberate absence of a network stack and of Internet connectivity (impossibility of browsing the web or exchanging packets).
Graphical resolution strictly frozen at 640x480 in 16 colours and audio limited to the PC Speaker.
Restricted physical hardware compatibility on modern computers (requires legacy BIOS mode, ATA and PS/2).
who_is_it_for: Students and researchers in computing history and in operating system architecture.
Developers curious to experiment with direct programming in HolyC and with the DolDoc documentary architecture.
Retro computing enthusiasts appreciating the simplicity and absolute hardware control of 1980s microcomputers.
Virtualisation enthusiasts wishing to explore an atypical system under QEMU or VirtualBox.
who_is_it_not_for: Users looking for an operating system for contemporary office work or web browsing.
Professionals and enterprises requiring a secure multi-user system with access rights management.
Modern video game players requiring 3D-accelerated GPU graphics drivers.
Internet-connected server infrastructures or cloud data centres.
content.verdict: TempleOS is an experimental operating system developed by Terry A. Davis. Stripped of modern abstractions, it includes its own language (HolyC), its shell, its compiler and a graphical environment, and constitutes a testimony on the design of unconventional operating systems.
